title: Master Lianchi: Seven Articles of Self-Admonition
author: Zhanran, annotated
excerpt: (The original text is taken from Posthumous Manuscripts of Master Yunqi: Self-Admonition.)

inline.s: The original text is taken from Posthumous Manuscripts of Master Yunqi
Self-Admonition
Karmic force that has gone unobserved is governing your life,
and its result is bound to be transmigration through the six realms;
but if you bring the power of vows into authority,
its result is then bound to be rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Mencius said:
"A person must first have that which he will not do, and only then can he do that which he will do."

(Translation: A person must first refrain from some things, and only then can he accomplish some things.) Human life is short and worldly affairs are boundless; for one who can accomplish great things, what is precious lies in the wise choice of goals and actions, and in the execution and perseverance of that choice. What one does is the great matter; what one refrains from is trivial. For a Buddha-reciter, one should take one mind undisturbed as the great matter, and the rest as trivial. Once one mind undisturbed has been reached, then one should cultivate the Buddha-recitation samādhi, taking seeing the mind and realizing the nature as the great matter, and the rest as trivial. Master Lianchi set us a brilliant example. We must each, according to our own actual situation and measured against the master's seven articles of self-admonition, formulate our own seven articles of self-admonition, and observe them from dawn to dusk,
with the single right thought

[Self-admonition] Self-warning, self-admonishment. In these seven articles of self-admonition, Master Lianchi clearly sets out which things must not be done, so as to preserve the single right thought.
Master Lianchi's "Self-Admonition" is now annotated as follows:

[The ancients had a saying: 'Yu cherished every inch of time; as for ordinary people, they should cherish every minute of it.' I am now old and decrepit; how could I merely cherish the minutes? Not even for the space of a finger-snap may I let my mind stray.]

The ancients said: 'Yu the Great, even though he was a sage, cherished every inch of time; we of this generation ought then to cherish every minute.' I am now advanced in years and feeble in body; how could I merely cherish the minutes? Not even for the space of a finger-snap may I let my mind stray.
[The ancients had a saying] The famous general Tao Kan of the Jin dynasty often said to people:
"Yu the Great was a sage, and yet he cherished every inch of time; we of this generation should cherish every minute."
[An inch of time] A brief span of time. The phrase comes from the Huainanzi, "Original Way":
"The sage does not value a foot-wide jade disc, but values an inch of time, for time is hard to gain and easy to lose."
[Time] Time, the passing of the hours. [A foot-wide disc] A jade disc one foot in diameter. [Disc of jade] Jade of the finest quality. [Xichi, xī chì] How much more than; not merely.

["Not letting the mind stray" means that, apart from the root-inquiry right thought, the moment a single stray thought arises, one must at once sweep it away and draw the mind back to the right thought, not delaying for a single moment.]
The so-called "

not letting the mind stray" means that, apart from the root-inquiry right thought, the moment a single stray thought arises, one must at once sweep it away and draw it back to the right thought, not delaying for a single moment.
[The root-inquiry right thought] Master Lianchi cultivated the Buddha-recitation samādhi through Chán inquiry, so his root-inquiry right thought was "Amitabha Buddha." Master Lianchi said:

"Raising the huatou is the most urgent and essential work for awakening in the Chan school. A practitioner of the Pure Land school takes the single sound of the Buddha's name as his huatou — this is a wondrous method."
He also said:
"When deluded thoughts are flying about in confusion, simply raise the Buddha
(the Buddha's name)
lightly once, and then stop; look — who is it that recites the Buddha's name? After a long while, if a thought arises
(if a deluded thought arises)
, raise it again in this way and look in this way; if no thought arises, simply keep looking."
(Collected Words on Pure Land by Master Yunqi) On Chán-inquiry Buddha-recitation and the Buddha-recitation samādhi, see in detail
Chán-Inquiry Buddha-Recitation
and
A Detailed Explanation of the Record of Groping the Image of the Buddha-Recitation Samādhi

[I now briefly set out seven matters. For those who have truly left home for the sake of birth and death and who wish to settle the great matter within this one life, they must strive to observe them and admonish themselves at all times.]

I now briefly set out seven matters. Those who have truly left home for the sake of birth and death and who wish to settle the great matter within this one life must do their utmost to observe them, admonishing themselves at all times.

[1. Do not hoard wealth, build houses, buy land, or acquire all manner of fine and exquisite things. Even sutras and images handed down from antiquity or produced by famous masters — do not cling to any of them; keep the single right thought.]

1. Do not hoard wealth, build houses, buy land, or acquire all manner of fine and exquisite things. Even sutras and images handed down from antiquity or produced by famous masters must not be clung to; keep the single right thought.
[The single right thought] Master Lianchi said:
"For one who aspires to learning, there is only one right thought, ever present in the chest. It is so in stillness, and so in bustle; let stillness and bustle shift as they will, and this
(same as 'this')

thought of mine never changes in the slightest. Only thus is there no interruption, and this is called being skillful in one's practice. Have you not seen how the ancients said: the wise remove the mind, the foolish remove the surroundings. If one insists on rejecting noise and seeking stillness, then I fear the surroundings will have no still moment and no still place. One who seeks stillness would go deep into the mountains. Yet even deep in the mountains it is still — but the woodcutter's axe is heard beyond the clouds and the herdboy's flute sounds in the slanting sunlight, so how can it be still at the ear? One might cut off the woodcutter's axe and the herdboy's flute so they never reach my ear; but in the clear night the gibbons cry and the tigers roar, and by day the magpies clamor and the crows caw — how can it be still then? One might drive away the gibbons and tigers and the magpies and crows so they never reach my ear; but when a wild wind rises and the myriad hollows roar in fury, and swift thunder breaks and the thousand mountains shake, then how will the one who rejects noise and seeks silence cut them off or drive them away? From this we may infer that the surroundings have absolutely no still moment and absolutely no still place. The student need only worry that his resolve is not fierce enough. With a fierce resolve, what can he not accomplish?"
(Collected Works of Master Yunqi)

[2. Do not engage in all manner of non-essential works of blessed karmic affinity. Wait until the great matter is clarified on some later day, and then it will not be too late to do them. For now, provisionally set aside the gate of the ten thousand practices, and keep the single right thought.]

2. Do not engage in all manner of non-essential works of blessed karmic affinity. Wait until the great matter is clarified on some later day, and then it will not be too late to do them. For now, provisionally set aside the gate of the ten thousand practices, and keep the single right thought.

[The great matter] Here it means seeing the mind and realizing the nature. For a Buddha-reciter who has not yet reached one mind undisturbed, single-mindedness in Buddha-recitation without confusion is the foremost great matter for ending birth and death. [The gate of the ten thousand practices] The "ten thousand practices" are all the methods of practice. "Gate" means that through which one enters and exits. Chan Master Guishan Lingyou said:
"In the ground of ultimate reality, not a single speck of dust is received; within the gate of the ten thousand practices, not a single dharma is abandoned."
(The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Guishan Lingyou of Tanzhou)

[3. Do not give rise to greed and craving toward pleasing sights and tastes, nor toward those who speak well of me and praise me. Do not give rise to anger and vexation toward ugly sights and bad tastes, nor toward those who speak ill of me and ridicule me, those who curse and insult me, and all manner of those who oppose me. Even toward past and future matters, whether agreeable or disagreeable, cut them all off entirely; fortify your walls and hold firm, and keep the single right thought.]

3. Do not give rise to greed and craving toward pleasing sights and tastes, nor toward those who speak well of me and praise me. Do not give rise to anger and vexation toward ugly sights and bad tastes, nor toward those who speak ill of me and ridicule me, those who curse and insult me, and all manner of those who oppose me. Even toward past and future matters, whether agreeable or disagreeable, all must be
cast aside and cut off
, without giving rise to thoughts of love and hate, grasping and rejecting; fortify your walls and hold firm, and keep the single right thought.
[Fortify the walls] Make the ramparts strong and firm.

[4. Do not compose poems and essays; do not write inscriptions, couplets, and scrolls in standard or cursive script; do not polish letters and correspondence; do not browse at leisure through non-Buddhist books; do not discuss the merits and faults, strengths and weaknesses of others; and do not, relying on mere personal opinion, write with a lofty heart, nor, when Chan is not yet penetrated, presume to cite and appraise the ancient cases. Seal your lips and hold your tongue, and keep the single right thought.]

4. Do not compose poems and essays; do not write inscriptions, couplets, and scrolls in standard script (the "true script") or cursive script, nor polish letters and correspondence ("chidu"); do not leaf through non-Buddhist books. Do not discuss the merits and faults, strengths and weaknesses of others; and do not, relying merely on personal private opinion, write in self-satisfied ("lofty-hearted") fashion. When Chan is not yet penetrated, do not presume to cite the ancient cases and appraise and promote them. You should seal your lips and hold your tongue, and keep the single right thought.

[Polishing letters] To revise and refine the wording of letters so as to make them perfect. [Non-Buddhist books] The Buddha's scriptural teachings are the "inner texts"; all books outside them are called "outer books." [Private opinion] One's own personal view. [Cite and appraise] Citing the ancient cases and appraising and promoting them. "Citing the ancient cases" is taking up an ancient gong'an to guide and transform the Chan student; "appraising and promoting" is to comment on and advocate the sayings of the ancients.
[5. Do not befriend relatives and acquaintances, accept invitations and attend social engagements, travel to admire the scenery, or engage in miscellaneous chatter and idle
(idle)

talk. Of all the various matters of the mundane world, apart from what principle requires one to do and what absolutely cannot be declined, set aside everything else, and keep the single right thought.]

5. Do not befriend relatives and acquaintances, attend engagements to which one is invited, travel to admire the scenery, or engage in miscellaneous chatter and idle talk. Of all the various worldly matters, apart from what principle requires one to do and what absolutely cannot be declined, dispense with all the rest, and keep the single right thought.
[6. Do not crave indulgence and laxity, nor give free rein to sleep. Before the great matter is clarified, endure toil and hardship, and keep the single right thought.]
6. Do not crave indulgence and lax pleasure, nor give free rein to sleep. Before the great matter is clarified, one must be diligent and endure hardship, and keep the single right thought.

[7. Do not compete with the world in talent and ability, contend for fame and power, claim to have attained what one has not attained, claim to have realized what one has not realized, falsely call oneself a spiritual teacher, or vainly exalt oneself. One should only hold to humility and abide in simplicity, dwelling all one's life in the position of a student, tempering oneself and ever advancing with diligence, keeping the single right thought.]

7. Do not compete with the world in talent and ability, contend for fame and power, claim to have attained what one has not attained, claim to have realized what one has not realized, falsely call oneself a good spiritual teacher, or vainly exalt oneself. One should only hold to humility and abide in simplicity, dwelling all one's life in the position of a student, tempering oneself and advancing without cease, keeping the single right thought.

[Claiming to have attained what one has not attained, claiming to have realized what one has not realized] To say that one has attained the holy Dharma when one has not, and to say that one has realized the fruit of the Way when one has not.
